utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good morning to everybody. May we hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any obstacles to immediately start with today's first witness, which would be if I count correctly number 56?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hopefully there are no obstacles, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From your side. And let me just check. No protective measures at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No protective measures for any of these witnesses today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then may I ask the usher to bring in Witness Sasa Milosevic. Is it Sasa or Sasa?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sasa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sasa Milosevic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind and give us your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You are a witness for the Defence. Please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, can you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sasa Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 10 February, 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Sijekovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where do you live today?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Sijekovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, you were ten, in March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened on the 26th of March, 1992? What happened to you and your family?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of March, 1992, around half past 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon, the Croatian army launched an attack on our village. I lived with my father, my mother, and my two brothers. Around half past 3.00, shells started falling on our houses. Ten minutes later, the army entered the village and started shooting at us. Together with my mother and my brother, I went to my neighbour's basement. My father and my older brother remained in our courtyard. Some 20 minutes later, the Croatian army entered the village, came to the cellar where we were, and they started swearing at us. They started beating us. We were there for some 10 minutes or so. Then they took us out from that basement with our hands behind our heads. They beat us with rifle butts. They kicked us with their legs, and then they -- we had to kneel in a hole, in a muddy hole. And then all the men were separated from the rest of the group, and they took me into a basement. And one of them told me: "I'm going to slay you now. I'm going to slaughter you." I started crying, and then he changed his mind and said I won't do it now. And then he told me to get up and start walking towards the main road. Then he told my 17-year-old brother to lay down on the ground. When he did that, he kicked him with an army boot. And there he remained on the ground lying on the ground. And when we started walking, he couldn't join us. And then Zemir Kovacevic started killing elderly people. The main person there was Nijaz Causevic, also known as Medo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the name of the person who started killing people immediately?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Zemir Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please continue.

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then we started walking towards the main road, and Zemir Kovacevic killed two people there. In my vicinity, maybe half a metre away from me, one of these two men was around 70 years old, and the other was a handicapped man. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Jovo Zecevic, and Petar Zecevic; a father and a son, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you taken after that?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After that, we were taken to a Croatian house. All of our neighbours were there. They were armed and they wore Croatian military uniforms with the HVO insignia. Nijaz Causevic came at that moment; he is also known as Medo. He took us to a public building. And he told us to wait there for a while. There were a lot of troops, of their troops there. And then Nijaz Causevic came again, and he tried to scare us by repeating his -- by cocking his rifle, by pointing his rifle at us. He told us: "Wait here for my return." And then a Muslim came. I don't know his first name, but his last name is [redacted]. And he took us to his place. And he told us: "Unless you come with me, you will all die." We stayed at his place, hidden at his place for two days. And then he transported us to the barricades in Derventa, and this is where we went.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, if you don't mind, I would ask for this name to be redacted. Actually -- the last name of the Muslim man, it's not in the transcript, but maybe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It would appear on line 21, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please redact from page 4, line 21, the first and the second name. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where did you go in Derventa? What side did you go to?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We went to the side where Serbs were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You and your mother went?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and all the other neighbours who were together with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did your mother -- what was your mother's ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: She was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to your father and to the brothers whom you had left behind in Sijekovac?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They must have been killed because I have never found out where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at Derventa, did you hear anything about this massacre in Sijekovac in the media?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We saw everything in -- on Jutel television, and I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. recognised some of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You recognised the bodies of the people that the Croat army did not manage to move away?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, but please remain in your place because maybe the Prosecutor and the Judges will have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I just have a couple questions for you. The neighbour that saved your life and helped you and your mother, you said he was a Muslim. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did he do that for money? Or did he do that on his own?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not for money. He did it on his own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You, Mr. Milosevic, were very young at the time. You still don't know for certain where your brother and where your father are, or where their bodies are. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court how it feels to have family members disappeared and never know what happened to them or where their bodies are?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It feels terrible. I would like to know at least where their graves are so that I can go there and light a candle for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only one additional question from my side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know by chance: Was there until now any prosecution in your home country against the offenders responsible for the crimes you described earlier today?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, there hasn't been any prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the follow-up question: Being aware that in your home country, these crimes are not prosecuted in a proper way or not prosecuted at all, it depends where the crimes have been committed and who are the responsibles now, the international society had decided to set up this Tribunal responsible for all, and I emphasise, all serious violations of international humanitarian law committed on the territory of the Former Yugoslavia since 1999. And therefore, there is a realistic possibility that in the future, your testimony as given today will be needed in other cases against the responsibles for the crimes you described today. Do you agree that this, what has been written down from your testimony, is used also in other cases?

utterances.speaker: SASA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Vassylenko. Judge Argibay. No further questions from our side. Then it remains for me to thank you, not only for coming, but also for giving testimony which is extremely important to see the balance, to see what happened on all sides. And it remains only for me to wish you a safe return and a better future in your home country. Thank you for coming. You're excused for today. May I ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, and goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence is prepared to continue with Witness 26, which would be Zarko Garic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Your Honour. Zarko Garic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we have to wait until the usher is able to bring in this witness. May I ask, any additional administrative matters to be settled in the meantime? Not from the side of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Nothing new, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nothing on our side right now, Your Honour. I just wanted to mention that this was the first our promised 15-minutes witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You announced this already the 16th of April, if I recall correctly, but you overstepped two minutes. Yes, may I ask, please, once again for a correction. On line 13, page 7, 1991 instead of 1999. One more technical question, the documents distributed yesterday, the testimony -- or the statements of the six persons, I don't know whether the Prosecution or the Defence want to have any protection; therefore, I don't want to quote the six names. But you're aware what I'm discussing right now. Are they tendered? Are these documents tendered by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: They are not tendered into evidence. They are given as the disclosures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is any party prepared to tender these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As I mentioned yesterday, Your Honour, I didn't have time to go through the documents, so I really cannot tell now. But hopefully, all of these witnesses would be testifying in front of this Chamber. So I don't know if it's necessary right now to have them tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It might be necessary in order to discuss them in detail. So therefore, I think the first right is for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we're not tendering statements not under oath, not given in oral evidence before the Court, and not according to the procedures of 92 bis as evidence. We're perfectly willing to discuss them, and if the Court wants to make them -- well, they are in the possession of the Court. We can discuss them, and if you want to give them a number or something. But we do not believe it would be proper to admit them into evidence because they don't come under any of the rules that allow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. This could be discussed, but I take it that for understandable reasons, the Defence wasn't able to read the entire documents until now. But we have to discuss this in the framework of our discussion tomorrow on the upcoming witnesses, no doubt, and therefore I ask all participants to be prepared to discuss this in detail. May I ask the registry, is it correct that the witness is scheduled to arrive only at 9.45?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So therefore, it's appropriate to have a break already now. And the trial stays adjourned until 10.00. --- Break taken at 9.27 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And may I ask the usher to bring in immediately the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Garic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You're a witness of the Defence. Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Garic. Will you just state your full name for the record, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: Zarko Garic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, 1950.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: Novo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where do you live?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: Donja Mocila.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Gornja or Donja Mocila?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: Gornja.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which municipality is that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened on the 3rd of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd -- I don't know about the 3rd of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of March, 1992, wasn't there an attack of the Croatian forces on Bosanski Brod? Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: I know that this happened in Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened on the 2nd of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: On that day, in the afternoon hours, Stevo Dejakovic [phoen] came, Kruna Blazevic [phoen], and they took me to the MUP building in Bosanski Brod. I was taken there. They gave me the uniform of captain first class of the Yugoslav army immediately, and I was put in an isolation cell. Later, I was taken for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I please interrupt you. Were you at that time captain first class of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: I never served in the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please continue.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: They asked me why I stayed and why I hadn't left the house alongside with the others, whether I was in possession of any weapons. They asked me that sort of thing. Night began to fall. I was returned to the isolation cell. Some people came over; I didn't know them. They said they had captured some Chetniks. And then they started beating me with rubber Bludgeon sticks, and that last about for about five or six minutes. The next morning, they took me out. My neighbours were there, and I was returned to my house around 12.00. When I came home, Nijaz Causevic, also known as Medo, had already killed our dogs. I then went to see my relative, Nedo. I spent the night there. And the next day, on the 4th, two policemen came along. They took me to the stadium camp, the camp that was on a football pitch. At the entrance, at the gate, Drago Lepan was waiting for me, and Pero Marinic, too. There was a man I didn't know, too. And they started beating me immediately. Once I had been beaten, I was put in one of the dressing rooms used by football players. There were about 13 or 14 of us there inside the dressing room. And as it was getting dark, they brought Milan Radovanovic, also known as Kuroga [phoen]. That man had a rather large head. People began to laugh at the expense of the size of his head. They started beating him. He was kicked and beaten and hit almost for the whole night. The next morning he was dead. Throughout the next days, there was training and songs and beatings, maltreatment. And they made us fight each other. After several days, we were taken out and taken to Sijekovac to load bags of sand, to do work for them. And this lasted until the 2nd of May. They brought me and my relative Nedo to Sijekovac, and some people wanted us to stay where we were and not to be taken. But we stayed there as part of this labour platoon. Something was read out to the effect that no one was supposed to beat us. We were about 50 or 60. There were both Muslims and Croats among the group. We started to do labour for them on a daily basis, to dig trenches, to chop wood. We helped repair the houses. We helped demolish houses, Serbian houses, and this was done on a daily basis. And then Nijaz Causevic started to come more often, a man also known as Medo. Zemir Kovacevic would also come, too, both Muslim, and then the torture started. They were the ones who beat us. The others didn't. And then when another man was brought -- I can't remember his name. I think it was Mustafa -- he was brought there, and he just looked and said: "What sort of criminals are these?" The work we did for them took about two months and ten days. Zemir Kovacevic, he came and took Neso Bacic [phoen] to Crni. He took Neso Bacic to Crni -- Savo Kusla [phoen] away, they never returned, not to this day. Medo Causevic, Nijaz, also known as Medo, would come. He came, and he said: "They are no longer here to do work." That he needed us, and that was already the 12th of July. He picked us up, put us into two vans - there were 18 of us - and took us to the Tulek camp. At the entrance, there was Alija Zenanic waiting for us. He took away our watches, personal documents, whoever had gold on them, and then we entered the compound of the camp. Once inside the camp, there was Drago Lepan waiting for me. And immediately, he wanted to hang me by my moustache. The next day, works began again. Trenches were dug. The Croatian army arrived. We went to dig trenches for them. This would usually last for about four or five hours, and then we would be returned. I returned, and Pero Marinic was there. He was a guard in this camp. He pulled out his gun as soon as he laid eyes on me, and he said: "This won't hurt a Serb." And then he kicked out my tooth, one of my teeth. And then on a daily basis, we continued to dig trenches. And on our way back, we would be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me please interrupt you for a moment. From what time exactly in the morning until when did you dig those trenches? Did this last for five hours, or did you return at 5.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: At 7.00 in the morning, we would be taken for the digging. Croatian soldiers would come and they would take us there to the trenches. And sometimes it would last for as long as -- late as 10.00 in the evening depending on the amount of work that was to be done and the trenches to be dug. At some point, Stuc Anto started to come to the camp. His nickname was Britva. He beat us the worst because he was using a baseball bat. Medo Causevic, I mean Nijaz Causevic, also known as Medo, he used to bring his people from the intervention platoon to rape women. Women would run to our group to hide among us occasionally so that we, too, would be beaten because we helped them to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was Djordjo Stojakovic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: Djordjo Stojakovic, he had been brought from Zagreb. He must have been 75 or 80 years old. A man who had been wounded in front of his own house in Derventa municipality. And he was brought among us with a tube down his throat, and that's where his wound was. After a couple of days, we were transferred from the Tulek camp to the Fric Pavlik camp. Djordjo stayed back at the Tulek camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. What was his nationality?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He had first been brought from Derventa in Bosnia and Herzegovina to Zagreb in Croatia, and then he was again returned to Bosanski Brod in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you continue, please.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: We were taken to the Fric Pavlik camp, but he stayed. We were a group of between 8 and 900 people. When we arrived there, the next day, the man who used to - in a manner of speaking - conduct us when we sang the songs they made us sing, as I've told you, Pajic, Mirko, I think, was his name. Then the International Red Cross arrived. Then he wrote something down on a slip of paper. He gave it to a woman who was there. How that came about, I don't know. Ante Golubovic, the camp commander, he came back with that same slip of paper. He read it out. He singled out four men. Three of them came back. Pajic was dragged back, but he expired within minutes. I was only kept there for four days. They would read out the names of a group of eight people. I was among them. And we were sent back to the Tulek camp. Once there, Djordjo was still in decent state, and we were told to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bury the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who were those dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: Serbs. There were all three ethnic groups. We buried the bodies of members of all three ethnic groups. Goran Garic, commander of the Tulek camp, Djordjo opened the big gate, and he let him go. In the morning, we found him in the garage at the graveyard. He was -- he had been all beaten. The tube was missing from his throat, and his wooden leg had been taken off, too. So we buried his body. That was our daily work. We would dig graves. We would then be returned to the Tulek camp, and we would always be beaten. Particularly severe beatings were administered by Ante Stuc, also known as Britva; Pero Marinic; Pero Cvorak. At night, they would come in a drunken state, and the guards would let them. There were night beatings, and during the day we would be taken to the graveyard. And this happened every single day. That's how it was. At the graveyard, I used to mow the grass. I only buried 22 Serb bodies. Perhaps 150 metres away from the graveyard, a large pit had been dug. I only saw it once. A yellow FAP truck brought bodies and tipped them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that the Orthodox cemetery where those bodies were tipped?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: No. That was at the far end of the cemetery which is not really the cemetery. Just next to the fence, that was passed the communist graveyard. I couldn't say exactly, but there was some bodies left in the truck because they didn't manage to tip them off the truck. So two Serbs went to drag the bodies down and to take their clothes off. Miro Kovacevic and Stanisa - I'm not sure about his last name. The other people there continued to bury the bodies, and I was transferred to graveyard maintenance. The Croatian graveyard, that is, the Catholic graveyard, the Muslim graveyard, as well as the communist graveyard. Only the Serb cemetery was not tended.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened on the 6th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of October, camp inmates were picked up in order to be taken to Croatia. The three of us, we were taken to the MUP building, just outside the MUP building, and we were forced to carry hand grenades to the bridge. And then a man I didn't know came along; he was drunk. He wanted to slit people's throats. He was asking about brothers; I'm not sure if he knew me or not. Anto Brekalo from Slavonski Brod - that's in Croatia - his task was to bring the three of us to Slavonski Brod. We were on the bridge until 6.30 or 7.00. They loaded us on to -- he loaded us on to his van, and he brought us home. He gave us dinner, because we were acquaintances. We had known each other. The three of us just sat there. He was there, too, with his wife. Then Croatian policemen broke into the house. They were looking for some people. They were asking him about those people, and he said: "The only people left are these three." And they picked him up, too, alongside with us, and took us to the camp near Bardak. Then he --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please just state again the name of the place they took you to.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: Camp near Bardak. That's a Serb house with a bowling alley, and there was a camp there. Brkelo was there. He had been detained with us. As soon as I came in, I had to have a fistfight with Sreto Radovanovic. Andrija Jozic made us fight, and Ivica Blazevic also known as Cedo. Brkelo's son said: "Admit old man, and you'll be taken to Orasje." Then eight other people came whom he had hidden so they could help with his bowling alley, the one recently built by Brkelo. Later, two buses arrived. We were a group of about 240 people. They took us as far as the buses, and then the police lined up in two lines, rows, and they beat everyone on their way to the buses. I carried a wounded man on a stretcher. He was quite heavy to lift and get on to the bus. So as I tried to get on to the bus, I was really beaten very badly. The buses set out, and Ivica Blazevic, also known as Cedo, was there -- he escorted us. He's a great friend of mine -- Andrija Jozic, and Zeljo Matkovic. We headed for Orasje via Zupljana. Once we reached Zupljana, Andrija Jozic showed up looking at the door looking for Zarko Garic to be out of the bus in 5 seconds. As soon as I got off the bus, there was a circle of men there consisting of some 7 to 8 people, and they started beating me immediately. And they used all sorts of things to beat me. I would fall down; they would lift me up. But I was still standing on my two feet, and then they got fed up by beating me and they asked two camp inmates to hold me and a third one to beat me. And one among the group said: "Hold on a little and I'll show you how an Ustasha from Herzegovina beats people." He hit me in the back of my head. I fainted, and I don't know how I arrived in Orasje. In the morning, when I came to, I couldn't move my arms or legs. They would take us out. I was taken out by two men. And then people were assigned either to stay in that camp or to be taken to another camp. Then women started throwing stones and potatoes at us, and other things. I was returned to the same place together with some other elderly people. I could not move for the next 12 days. A priest entered the room, and he brought us a hundred packs of cigarettes. All of the others stood up to shake hands with him. I couldn't do that. And he asked me what the matter was with me. And then the others told him: "Well, he fell off the lorry." And that was the usual answer. Every wounded person was instructed to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you for a moment. That priest, was that a Catholic priest? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. He said I should be taken to the doctor's. I was taken to the doctor's. He gave me some pills. I don't remember the name of those pills, and he gave me an ointment because I was all black and blue. After having taken those pills, after a massage, I was taken together with the others to dig trenches. We went out for two or three days, and then we were transferred to the Mahala camp. There, I stayed with all the others, and we continued going out to work. And then I was taken to a place called Gajovi to work, to unload a tractor full of logs. The driver was afraid to drive through that area because it was in the line of bullets from both sides. He was afraid. He asked me to drive although I don't have a driving license, he told me: "Don't you worry, just press your foot on the gas pedal and drive on." And I indeed drove the tractor to the place where I was supposed to drive it to. I got off the tractor, and he shot a bullet at me. And I was hit by a fragmentation bullet, and I was wounded in my hip and in my finger. I did not have any anything to dress the wound with. And two men told me: "Come with us. Our house is very close and we will deal with that. We will help you." We turned to the house, there was a girl there, and there was another man there as well. When he looked at my finger -- actually, there was no finger at all. He told me: "Okay, let's deal with that as best as we could," although we did not have any anaesthetics. I lay down. One of the men sat on my chest; the other one sat on my legs. And then they started treating my finger. I almost died there with the suffering. It didn't last long. I only heard the hissing of a spray. He sprayed the wound with something. This was done by people who were not supposed to do something like that. Later on, a doctor came. I actually don't know whether he was a doctor, but in any case, he told the two men that they would be held responsible for what they had done to me. Then they took me back to the camp without giving me any tablets or anything. I stayed in bed with my hand in the air. That is the only position in which I felt comfortable. And that lasted until the 14th of November. At 9.00 in the evening, from -- the 11 of us from Bosanski Brod Municipality were loaded on to a van and transported across the Sava River to Croatia. There, we were put in the same camp at Bardak as before. There, we found in one of the two rooms 11 of us were in one part of the basement, and in the other part of the basement, there were 32 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. other people. The others would be taken out to do some work, such as washing cars and other things, if things had to be transported or something. They did not take me out of the cellar, as I was wounded. And then we were taken to be exchanged on the day that I don't remember. We were transported towards Draganic in Croatia near Zagreb. And then they released only two women, and all the rest of us men were taken back at the Bardak camp. On the 19th of December, Tomo Aracija, my neighbour, came. And when he saw me and when he saw the condition I was in - and he was the one in charge of exchanges - he said he would leave his position and stop doing his job if I wasn't exchanged. On the 21st of December, the -- a policeman came, just one policeman came, looking for Zarko Garic. I said I was Zarko Garic. And he said: "Come out and sit in the Land Rover." I did that. He started the engine and drove off, and I don't know where we were going. He asked me if I liked music, and I said yes. So he put the radio on. I asked him: "Where are you taking me?" He said: "I'm taking you to be Kobasij to be exchanged." And to my greatest fortune, the exchange was successful. I was taken to my native village. My house wasn't there any longer. Everything had been burned down. And on the following day, I transported to Serbia to a hospital there. And I was hospitalised for five and a half months. And that would be all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] We don't have any further questions, Your Honour. So the Prosecution can proceed. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You told us your impressive story this morning. Leaving, for a moment, aside all legal and formal perspectives, from your own perspective, whom do you, yourself, hold responsible for that what happened to you, on the lower level, on the middle level, and on the highest level of the hierarchy, when looking back?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: To me personally, and to other people in Sijekovac, the responsible person is Nijaz Causevic, also known as Medo. He was the one who committed the greatest crimes against us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was his capacity in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: He was not in the municipality; he was in Sijekovac, in the school. We grew up together. He was retired as a very unstable person, and he rallied around himself all the people very similar to him. And they called themselves the "intervention platoon." They were nothing but thieves, thieves from Baghdad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that there was any organisation behind, or was it more or less a crime committed by those persons mentioned by you earlier in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever testified in another case in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the first time I have testified before any court of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I, in addition, ask: Do you know anything about a prosecution of those persons you mentioned today allegedly responsible for the crimes committed not only against you, also against others you mentioned? Was there any kind of prosecution on the territory of Former Yugoslavia you would know about?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: Nijaz Causevic has been convicted, and he had committed crimes before the war. He killed his first-door neighbour, and he was never taken to account for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The international community is aware of the flaws of prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international and humanitarian law committed in the territory of Former Yugoslavia since 1991. Therefore, this Tribunal is established. And it may be necessary to make use of your testimony in another case against the responsible persons. Do you agree that what was written down as your testimony today will be used in other cases as well?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO GARIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any additional questions? Judge Vassylenko. Judge Argibay. Then I have to thank you not only for coming, but also for your testimony. We all are aware how difficult it is to testify here. It opens, once again, the wounds. But I think it will help, and it will assist in bringing once again peace to your home country that people live together peacefully. I thank you for your own contribution to this. You're excused for today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to escort the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, Madam Registrar, the scheduling for the next witness? When will he or she arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I was just informed the witness was on his way. Should be here in about 5 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's take the opportunity. And the trial stays adjourned until 11.20. --- Break taken at 10.50 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I ask the usher to bring in Nikola Cikojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Witness Cikojevic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Cikojevic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Nikola Cikojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: 7 March, 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: In Slavonski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: I live in Srpska Brod, in a village called Gornji Mocila, in the local commune called Sijekovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you live there on the 3rd of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I lived in Sijekovac village, actually in Gornji Mocila village, Sijekovac local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you know about the 3rd of March, and how you organised your life after that.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of March, the Croatian army of the Republic of Croatia stormed in to Bosanski Brod municipality. The military government was set up in Bosanski Brod after that. The civil authorities stopped working in Bosanski Brod Municipality. And the Croat/Muslim government put up the military police checkpoints. And there were checks, people were brought in and ill treated. I worked in the Bosanski Brod oil refinery. And my aunt who was one of the foremen in the company asked me to come to Brod and to stay with her in her house. And she also told me that the government ordered everybody to go back to work. I managed to pass all the checkpoints. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. arrived in Brod. I arrived at my aunt's house on the 18th of March. And after that, I didn't dare show my face in the street or move around. While I was staying there, on the 25th of March, I was sitting in a room overlooking the street. It was around 1700 hours when I heard an explosion. There was an explosion followed by noise and shouting. I saw people running across the street. I could also hear shots. And after that night, on the following morning, a neighbour of Serbian ethnicity came knocking at our door, at the door of my aunt's house. My aunt opened the door, and that lady, the neighbour, entered the house, and asked my aunt: "Neighbour, what is going on?" And she also said: "Did you know that Andrija Martic had been killed as well as his son, as well as their neighbour Dujanic, who was staying in their house at the time."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what was the ethnic background of these people?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs. And Momir Martic's wife, Merima, who was a Muslim, and the late Dujanic's brother were seriously injured, the two of them. And that's how we spent that day up to the evening. We put the TV on, and we watched the news. And on the news, I saw my village. And I could see that my Serbian neighbours had been slain. The Zecevic family, the Milosevic family, and the Radanovic family, and the Trifunovic family as well. And then they showed again footage of the 27th on Jutel. They showed Biljana Plavsic, Fikret Abdic, and I think there was Boras on behalf of the Croatian side. They showed Serb bodies, people who had been killed on the 26th. I knew the deceased Luka Milosevic and his son, Zeljo. Their bodies were lying in the garden. That was all in the period preceding the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please allow me to just remind you, what happened on the 7th of May?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of May, my mother remained in the village. In our house, the house where we lived. She didn't manage to escape when those people from Sijekovac withdrew to the Serbian village of Zboriste. She had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened on the 9th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, the family house was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was it that set your house ablaze?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Our neighbours did, because there was no one else around. Serbs had been detained or they had escaped from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your neighbours who set fire to your house, what was their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: They were Croats. My village was a mixed one, Serbs and Croats living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened on the 14th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of May, after the JNA had withdrawn, that was on the 11th of May, and then on the 14th, my aunt's neighbour found out that I was staying with my aunt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity, the neighbour's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was a Croat. Ferdo Kljajic. He told me to go and report to the military authorities in Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you report on that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, the same day. My aunt, her daughter, and myself. As I was the only male, I had just turned 18, but they wouldn't let me go alone because they were afraid to let me go on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So when exactly did you report?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: We reported to the Unipromet company building. Pero Lepan was there. He was in charge. He was the head of that particular work unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What tasks were you assigned as part of your work in that work unit, and where did you spend your nights?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: We would stay in the work unit between 7.00 in the morning and 8.00 in the evening. We had to bring our own food from where we stayed, from our homes, because they didn't give us any food there. And in the town, there is this new district, Brodsko Polje. We replaced the tiles and the construction materials from the roofs of houses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you replace those or remove them?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: We removed the tiles from Serb houses, the windows, too. And since this was a new district, we removed construction materials from the building plots, and then we would take these construction materials to the central warehouse set up by Croatian military authorities in the town. While I was in the work unit, they sent me to the graveyard to dig graves for three or four days. That's where I buried the first bodies from -- the bodies of the first victims from the village Poloje, the village of Poloje. After the JNA had withdrawn, these people were killed, and they were Serbs, elderly Serbs, men and women.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember any of their names?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Petrovic, I believe, Jelka Petrovic. I don't know about the man. Petrovic. And there was someone named Kalabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did they treat you in your work unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: They did maltreatment us occasionally. Sometimes they would swear at us and beat us. Also in May, they took us to the stadium, the town stadium to repair the roof. There was a camp there, a camp for Serbs. There were some military police garrisoned there, the Brod Brigade. And as we were waiting there to go and repair the roof, the inmates were working. And on one occasion, one of the inmates was clearing some shards of glass. A shell had fallen there and shattered the glass. From the back, he was approached by Jasenka Bilic and Manda Djakovic. They started cursing his Serb mother. "Are you stupid or what? Can't you do it a bit faster?" He said he couldn't work any faster. At that point, Tadija Lepan walked up to him and started beating him. He threw him from the floor down in front of the building. Three people came down, and Drago Lepan was with them, too. And another blond rather short and plumpy military policeman. I can't remember his name. They continued to beat him. We climbed up to the roof at that point, and I don't know what happened to him later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When exactly were you taken and detained in the Tulek camp?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of June, in the morning, when I came to the Unipromet headquarters, the military police came to get me and Predrag Vrac. They took us to the Tulek camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they seize anything from you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they seized my watch, my gold necklace, and my personal documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What sort of treatment were you given in that camp?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: When Vrac and I arrived there, there were between 15 and 20 Serbs there who had already been detained. There was a woman there in that group. We were given assignments there to work with cement. They were building a prison; a prison was to be built. We spent two or three days working there. And then they started to take us elsewhere to dig trenches. Tadija Lepan was the person in charge of singling out prisoners to take them away to dig trenches and his uncle, Drago Lepan, and a number of other persons, but I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In early July, did they bring any other people to the Tulek camp?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Early July, they brought people from Derventa, about 140 -- 130 of them, men and two women. One of them was a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After a number of days, were people from Odzak brought over, too?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in deed. After Odzak had fallen, they brought in people from Odzaci, both women and children. While they were there in the camp, the Tulek camp, every day, Croat and Muslim forces, military policemen, would come to beat people, and members of the army, too, would beat people. In early July, a Muslim woman was brought there. She was from Kozarac, near Prijedor originally. During that period, Zdravko Marinic and Zoran Cavraja were the persons in charge. They were playing cards. They were on duty. And they were placing bets that whoever lost the game would go there and rape this particular Muslim woman. In that part of the barn, we heard a conversation they were having. They were making a lot of noise apparently quarrelling. At one point they came up to me and they Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. told me: "Look, now you'll go there and abuse that Muslim woman sexually. All right"? I told them I couldn't. "Kill me if you want to, but I'm not going to do that." They gave up on me, and they made Slobodan Jandric from Sipovo, who had been brought to the camp from the Republic of Croatia, the Tulek camp, with three other Serbs who worked in Rijeka. While we were in the Tulek camp, Drago and Tadija Lepan used to come quite frequently. They forced the people from Derventa and Odzaci to sing the "Jure I Boban" Ustasha anthem. In early July, Tadija Lepan's father was killed. Drago Lepan came to the Tulek camp. His mother and children. Drago knocked down the gate, the door to the room where the prisoners from Derventa were kept and he, his mother, and the children started beating people in there. Then he came to our barn where people from Brod were being kept. He started beating everyone. He beat me, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were two Croat men together with you detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Boro Jankovic and his father. I can't remember the father's name now. Boro's mother was a Serb. She had fled with the younger son who was not yet a military-aged man. They had run with the Serbs, but the two of them stayed in their house. And when Serbs were being picked up across Brusnica, which is again a mixed village, Croats and Muslims, then the two of them were picked up. They maltreated them more than us Serbs actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened on the 9th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: The 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that the day the International Red Cross arrived?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's when I was first recorded by the International Red Cross, registered. They stormed into the camp, and they saw people inside, and they requested to enter so that they could see who was being kept in there. And that's when the International Red Cross took our names and registered us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like now to ask you to tell me about late July 1992. Were you transferred to a different place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: In late July -- in late July, Serbs from Derventa and Odzaci were transferred to the Gik warehouse. It was a construction material warehouse used by the Gik, G-i-k, company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the Tulek camp?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: We stayed until the 17th [as interpreted] of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the date again.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: The 18th of August, 1992. We were transferred to a school, because the International Red Cross had announced that they would come, so they picked up the few of us who were able-bodied men from Odzak, Brod, and Derventa, took us to the school gym, which was in a school. The elderly, sick, wounded, women, and children were being hidden, concealed, and moved. And they also moved the people from the stadium to the kayak club. They hid them. They concealed them from view because the International Red Cross had not registered these people the first time they came. We stayed there for four days. And during those four days, one person was killed. During the visit of the International Red Cross, an inmate from Derventa wrote down a message on the slip of paper and handed the slip to a lady from the International Red Cross. He asked her not to give him away. He wrote down where the wounded and sick and women and children were being kept, concealed from view. This lady went to see the camp commander. He was a military policeman by the name of Golubovic. She asked him where the socks factory was. And he replied: "What?" And then she said that she had obtained information that they were keeping Serbs there. After the International Red Cross people left the camp, Zdravko Ostojic came. He singled out four persons from Derventa for questioning. He wanted to find out who had provided the information on the Serbs who had been hidden from view. They sent back three of these persons, and Mirko Pajic was held back. Zdravko Ostojic came up to us and said: "He wasn't clever enough to save his own life. He must write up a report regarding his actions." After two hours, Anto Golubovic and his deputy took Mirko Pajic, his deputy's name was Tolic, their arms around each other's shoulders, and in the gym they said: "No one here is allowed to touch you. You're a very good friend of ours." And then they walked away from him and started to beat people in front of all of us there in the hall. And then they asked him: "Will you now admit whether you were the one who gave away the location of those who had been hidden to the International Red Cross?" He couldn't answer because he had already fallen unconscious. He was taken out again. And then after an hour, they were back to get me and another man. We were supposed to carry his body back into the building. They ordered the doctor from Derventa, the lady doctor, to go there and have a look. They told her that apparently he had come down with the flu and maybe he had a slight fever. I was standing just there, and the doctor said: "This man can't be helped. He's finished." And after about one hour, the man died. A van came to take the body away. Myself and three other people took the body to the graveyard. Two days later, we buried him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that secondary school?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you then transferred to?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: We were sent back to the Tulek camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do there upon your return?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Eight of us were assigned to dig graves at the town cemetery, to bury Serbs who had been killed. Those men had been digging trenches and getting killed because they were in the line of fire, also Croats and Muslims. We buried all the bodies that were brought to the graveyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you then also maltreated and beaten?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, two or three times. At the Muslim cemetery, all eight of us were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long were you detained in the Tulek camp?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: While we were there, or working at the town cemetery, let me just add this: The Bardak family was brought there. A man, his wife, and his mother-in-law. His name was Branko, and I don't know the women's names. He was a man -- he was a working man. He had his own company. They came to their house. They tied their hands, gagged them, and slit their throats. When they were brought to the cemetery, I saw it with my own eyes the way their hands had been tied, the way they had been gagged, and their throats slit. I buried them with my own hands. Also, a soldier from the stadium was captured, Jovo Dujic. He was also brought to the cemetery. I saw with my own eyes that his nose and ear had been cut off. I buried him, too. And I also buried Djordjo Stojakovic. A man called Jeremas [phoen], who was a director in a company in Brod, he was also killed. He was a prominent figure in Brod. And I really can't remember the names of all those whom I buried. It has been a long time since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the Tulek, and where were you transferred from there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: I stayed at the Tulek camp until the 6th of October, until the fall of Brod. And then around 2.00 in the afternoon, they took us to the bridge. There we waited for the group of those who had stayed behind in the centre and at the stadium. And while we were crossing the bridge, they also ill treated us, they also beat us. Once we crossed the bridge, in the column in front of me, people were killed. And I came across the dead body of a female detainee from the stadium. I believe that her name was Desanka. She was a Serb from Teslic. I saw with my own two eyes Kadija Nibic killing her with a pistol. There was another man who shot at her, but I don't know his name. It all happened on the bank of the River Sava in the Republic of Croatia. And then we arrived at a Serb house, Bardak, also known as the bowling alley, in Slavonski Brod in the Republic of Croatia. There we stayed until 11.00 in the evening. All throughout that time, they beat us, they cursed us, and they maltreated us. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. At 11.00, two buses came. 240 of us were loaded on to those buses, and they drove us to Zupljana in the Republic of Croatia. They brought us to the bank of the Sava River. The door of the bus opened, and Zarko Garic was taken off the bus. He was beaten there. Later on, they took the rest of us off --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what happened there.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: They -- they took us, actually forced us, to go to the ferry that served to transport people and livestock across the river. And while we were being transported, they beat us. It was the military police and the army of the Republic of Croatia and the Croat Defence Council members who beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay there and where were you transferred next?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: We were brought to Mahala village in Orasje municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. What did you do in Orasje?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: In Orasje, we arrived on the 7th, around 4.00 in the morning, and they placed us in a big hall. They ill treated us. They beat all of us up. And in the morning, they took us out to the schoolyard in Mahala. Again, they beat us there and asked if there was anyone sick in the group. And if there was, that that person should step out from the line. Those who were sick and wounded stepped out of the line, and then the commander of the Orasje camp started interrogating us. His name was Pera Vincetic, and he was also known as Konj. And that's what we heard. That's what we heard his nickname was, Konj, or horse. And they beat us there. The villagers came, threw things at us, cursed our Serb mothers. A soldier asked Pera: "Will you sell me 30 of the inmates?" And Pera said: "No, they are my slaves." They split us into groups, and they kept only 60 of us who were fit to work. And the rest of the group was taken to Orasje. Four women who were brought together with us from Brod also remained with our group. We were sent to dig trenches. And when we returned to the camp compound, they would beat us day in, day out. And during the night hours, they would come to fetch the women, and they would take them out to be raped one at a time. I'm not going to mention any of their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, when were you transferred to Slavonski Brod from Orasje?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: We were transferred from Orasje to Slavonski Brod on the 16th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you beaten there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in Slavonski Brod, we were not beaten, but the conditions were very bad. We were placed in a cellar with sewage pipes going through that cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was the first attempt of your exchange?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 24th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the exchange -- was the exchange successful?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. They took us back to Slavonski Brod. This is where we stayed throughout that winter. We didn't have any warm clothes, and the winter was very severe with temperatures down to minus 23. We had to do very difficult physical work. And once a day, they would give us a meager ration of food until March 1992 [as interpreted] --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was in March 1993. And then we started working for the commander of the military police, Anto Suger. We worked on his private property until 26th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you transferred on the 26th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: We were transferred to Ljubuski in Herzegovina, that is Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: We were assigned to dig trenches on the Nevesinje front line, and they were taken there by the military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the distance between Ljubuski and Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did it take you to get there? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: We travelled via Slavonska Pozega, Zagreb, Karlovac, down to Split. We were in the Lora harbour. That's where we had lunch, and then we continued on our journey, and we arrived around 7.00 or 8.00 in the evening. And we started the journey around 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was the second attempt of your exchange?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 4th of July, 1993. We were transported to Livno. There, we waited for some three hours, and then they took us back to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they beat you in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't beat us in Ljubuski. We were assigned to dig trenches on the Nevesinje and Trebinje front lines for three or four days. And the rest of the time, we worked in the transit warehouse. But the Muslims who were there were maltreated because the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats had started. They didn't touch us, but they did ill treat the detained Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was the third attempt of your exchange?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 16th of July, 1993. We were taken to a place called Celebici, and that is when I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the total duration of your imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Over a year. A year and a few more days. I don't know exactly how many more days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cikojevic. I have no further questions, but maybe my learned friend from the Prosecution and the Honourable Judges will have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Cikojevic, thank you for coming and telling us about your experiences. One of the experiences you told us about was when you were asked, in fact, you were threatened -- someone tried to get you to commit a crime, to rape this woman, Muslim woman, from Kozarac. And you refused to do that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: I refused. I couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Even though you were 18 years old and in prison, you refused when someone tried to get you to commit a crime because it was wrong and it was against your conscience. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I couldn't do it. It was against my conscience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you think if more people in Bosnia had stood up against those who tried to encourage them to commit crimes against other ethnicities and had said no, that a lot of what happened in that war would not have occurred?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't fully understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Cikojevic, if more people had done what you did and refused to commit crimes against innocents just because they were of another ethnicity, do you think that the war in Bosnia would have been very different, or Bosnia would be very different then and today?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that it would be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: One of the things you talked about was efforts by people running the camps to keep the International Red Cross from visiting and from learning particularly about the presence of women in those camps.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly what was done. They tried to prevent them from coming. And when I was registered for the time, it was a surprise visit to the Tulek camp. And then the person who was our guard, the military policeman, opened the door, he saw people inside moving around. And he said: What is that?" So when he saw them, he just disappeared, and then they approached us. They came up to us and asked us what was going on. We told them that we were just detained there, that everything -- all of our possessions had been taken away and that we were just sitting there. Nobody -- when we first came, nobody ever told us anything. They just collected our identification documents, and they just held us there and we didn't know what we were doing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Cikojevic, can you tell us, why would authorities, political leaders who had set up camps, want to keep the International Red Cross and international community from visiting those camps?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was not the political authorities but the military authorities in Bosanski Brod. From 3rd of March 1992 onwards, so it was the military component that took over. It was the 108th Slavonia Brigade, and the commander of that brigade would visit us in the camp. He came two or three times to the camp. So it was not the civilian authorities, but the military authorities. And that was from the 3rd of March, 1992, onwards. So the civilian authorities stopped existing on the 3rd of March in Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So in Brod, the people with authority over the camps in Brod at that time was this military authority from the HVO. Why would they want to keep the International Red Cross and the international community from visiting camps and registering the inmates? Explain it to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You should ask them. Why did they do that? Probably they were afraid of the truth. They were afraid of what was going on and the truth to be known.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When prisoners were registered, did you feel some sense of security that at least your name was on record and that you would not simply disappear with no record of your name ever having existed in that camp?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: I did feel a bit safer, but when the International Red Cross representatives left, nothing changed. The same ill treatment continued. People were still being taken to dig trenches despite the fact that the International Red Cross insisted with the military authorities that they shouldn't take us to dig trenches on the front line where people were being killed every day. Still, Mirko Pajic, he was registered with the International Red Cross, but he was still killed. And this happened after their visit, so this feeling of security was false. We couldn't really be safe. Our life was on the line day in, day out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You talked -- I just want to go back for a moment. This woman, the Muslim woman that they asked you to rape. You said she was from Kozarac. Do you know how she ended up -- I believe -- was that in Slavonski Brod at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, it was in Tulek, in Bosanski Brod, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know how she happened to find herself in the camp. But I know that she was detained together with another woman from Brod, and there were other women and men who were brought in. But they were exchanged from time to time. But these two ladies stayed with us for a longer time. One of them was over 60, and the Muslim woman who was around 30 at the time. She was a bit -- she was simple. She was a bit retarded, if you know what I mean. She was not a full dozen. And they would rape on a regular basis. It was the army troops who did that and the military police who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I also want to go back to what you saw on television from Jutel of the visit of the presidency of Bosnia to the massacre site, the village in Sijekovac. Forgive me if I --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Sijekovac, yes, that's the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At that time, the people that visited were members of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was Mrs. Plavsic from the SDS; Mr. Abdic at that time, from the SDA; and you said also a Croat was present. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe his name was Boras, but I can't remember his first name. And they were three representatives of the three different peoples, and it was an attempt to reconciliate these people at that time, at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So at that time, it was an attempt to say that the people of Bosnia don't want to see this kind of events, massacres of innocent civilians, occur again?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a meeting arranged to take place in Brod. I think it was on the 9th of March, 1992. This is what was arranged in the presidency. In Brod, they didn't actually -- they were not aware of the massacre in Sijekovac. They just came by it because the bodies had not been taken away. They just came. They saw it. And there is a footage of that. A month and a half ago, I saw the footage again. The footage was made by a Croat whose daughter was employed by the television in Brod. He edited that for himself. I saw the footage, but it is not the same footage that was shown on Jutel. Some things were redacted, taken out from that footage. It's a different footage that I saw this time. So the footage was not the complete footage that aired on the 27th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said that what you saw at that time was from Jutel. That was a television station broadcasting from Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And in that broadcast, it showed the images of the victims of the massacre?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Houses burned and bodies of people who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At that time in Brod, could you also receive television from Banja Luka? I don't believe there's television in Prijedor, but from Banja Luka or from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: The signal was very feeble, so you couldn't see actually TV Banja Luka. At least where I was spending my days, I couldn't see TV Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How about the television from Belgrade? Were you able to see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we could see TV Belgrade, but not where I was. We could only watch TV Sarajevo and TV Zagreb. In Bosanski Brod, you had TV Belgrade, too, but personally I was not able to locate the right frequency on my own TV set.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Had you seen on any of these television programmes images about what occurred after the fall of Vukovar in Croatia and what happened at the hospital there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not really. I didn't really follow that much when there was the war in Croatia. So I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see any television -- you mentioned Mrs. Plavsic. Did you see any television reports of her in I believe it was Bjeljina where she kissed Arkan?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I know nothing of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cikojevic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned during your testimony that your camp where you were detained was visited two or three times by the commander of the 108th Slavonia Brigade. And can you tell us when this was and can you give us the name of this commander?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: I only know that he had the rank of colonel, but I don't know his name. This was approximately in late June or early July.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, 1992. And there were regular military forces, too, while we were doing digging in Brod. I forgot to mention that. There was the Rijeka Brigade, the Bjelovar Brigade, the Osijek Brigade, the Karlovac Brigade, and another of the engineering brigades. They monitored us as we were digging the trenches. They came midway through July 1992 and stayed until the fall of Brod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Totally different question: Did you ever see columns of fugitives coming from the war in Croatia in your hometown?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I did see the Serbs fleeing Slavonski Brod, fleeing the Republic of Croatia back in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In which direction did they flee?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: From Croatia into Bosnia, because that's the lie of the land. When we had Yugoslavia, still the Former Yugoslavia, many Serbs had moved out of the village of Poloje. There were over 500 houses in that village, and those Serbs moved to Bosanski Brod because that was just next to the River Sava. In Slavonski Brod, in the Republic of the Croatia, they built a town district, a settlement, call Bijelis. But they lived all over Slavonski Brod municipality, the Serbs, I mean. Many people, 70 per cent of Bosnians, worked in Croatia, in Slavonski Brod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you personally ever been in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: No -- well, I did pass through once when I was taken to be exchanged in 1993. The route we took was Grahovo, Drvar, Petrovac, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Banja Luka, and then via Derventa on to Brod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In passing Prijedor, did you see something special, to the best of your recollection, you regard as worth mentioning here?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA CIKOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what to mention. I've nothing particular to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
